verses.translation_literal: A psalm for thanksgiving. Shout in acclamation to YHWH, all [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm, for the giving of thanks. Lift your voices to the LORD: let the whole earth raise the cry!
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening cry is not a polite hymn. The verb hari'u comes from the root ruaʿ, the sound of the trumpet blast and the war-shout, and it is also what a crowd does to acclaim a king at his enthronement. Play it as a roar, a whole assembly on its feet. The KJV 'make a joyful noise' captures the volume, but 'joyful' is its own addition, and 'noise' makes the command sound faintly grudging; the Hebrew simply says 'shout to YHWH'.

The heading matters as much as the first line. The KJV calls the psalm 'a Psalm of praise', but the word is todah, thanksgiving, and the same word comes back in verse 4 ('with thanksgiving', betodah), where its root sounds again in hodu, 'give thanks to him'. A todah was a specific act: someone who had been rescued from sickness, danger or the sea came to the sanctuary, offered a thanksgiving sacrifice and told the story to everyone present (Targum: 'a praise over the thanksgiving offering'; Rashi: said over the sacrifices of thanksgiving). The psalm is the script for that crowd. 'All the earth' can also be 'all the land', as the KJV 'all ye lands' sees; Ibn Ezra reads it as a collective noun for all who live on it. In the Hebrew numbering the heading is part of verse 1; the KJV counts it as verse 0.

philological_notes.note: 'For thanksgiving': todah is both the spoken confession of what God has done and the sacrifice that accompanies it. It is not the general 'praise' of the KJV heading (that would be tehillah, as in verse 4). Rashi takes it as the psalm said over the thanksgiving offerings, and the Targum reads it as a praise over the offering.
Hiphil imperative of ruaʿ: to raise the shout, the war-cry or trumpet-blast, and the acclamation of a king. Malbim connects it to the royal acclamation of God (Ps 47:2).

verses.translation_literal: Serve YHWH with joy; come before his face with a ringing cry.
verses.translation_dramatic: Serve the LORD, and let joy be the sound of your service. Come into his presence, come before his very face, and let your coming be a song.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs of movement frame the verse: 'serve' and 'come'. 'Serve' (ʿavad) is the word for a slave's labor, a subject's service to a king, and the priest's work at the altar. Here the actors should hear all three together: this is duty, not leisure, and the surprise is that it is to be done with joy. The traditional commentators felt the tension. Ibn Ezra says that it is the habit of every servant to be sad, so the psalm asks for joy and not for a hidden service; Malbim says the difference lies in the reward, since service to a man brings pay afterward, but service to God is its own reward.

The KJV 'before his presence' blurs a Hebrew idiom that is much more physical: lefanav is literally 'to his face'. In the sanctuary one 'sees the face' of God, which is to say one appears before him as a petitioner appears before a king. The last word, rinanah, is the ringing shout of joy, a cry more than a tune; the KJV's 'singing' makes it quieter and more orderly than it is. Rashi adds a polemical edge: those who serve idols cannot serve with joy, since idols pay no wages.

philological_notes.note: 'Serve': the verb for a slave's or a subject's labor and for cultic service. The psalm sets it beside joy deliberately; Ibn Ezra and Malbim both comment on how unusual that pairing is.
Literally 'to his face'. To appear 'before the face' of YHWH is the standard idiom for entering the sanctuary; 'presence' (KJV) is correct in sense but loses the physical image.

verses.translation_literal: Know that YHWH, he [is] God; he made us, and to him [belong] we, his people and the flock of his pasture.
verses.translation_dramatic: Know this, and know it well: the LORD, he alone is God. He made us. We are his, his people, the flock he feeds in his own pasture.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm and the only verse that gives a reason, and it begins with a command to know. In Hebrew 'know' (yadaʿ) is not mere information but recognition, a confession. 'YHWH, he is God' has the stress of the declaration on Mount Carmel: this must be said as a statement against rival claims, not as a pleasant thought. The pronoun 'he' is doubled, 'he is God, he made us', which the actors can use as two hammer-blows.

The famous textual trap is in the middle. The consonants of the text read lo' ('and not'), but the scribes' reading tradition says lo ('to him'). The KJV follows the written form: 'and not we ourselves', which turns the line into a denial of self-creation and has colored English-language devotion ever since. Most modern translations, and the ASV, YLT and BBE here, follow the reading: 'and we are his'. Radak and Meiri both discuss the written 'not'; Meiri notes that the 'not' reading is a denial of Ezekiel 29:3, where Pharaoh says 'I made myself'. Both readings are defensible, but the Qere fits the next clauses, which are all about belonging: 'his people, the flock of his pasture'. In the ancient Near East a shepherd-king who owned a flock was responsible for feeding and guarding it; the metaphor ties ownership and care together, as Meiri notes ('his pasture shows his providence over us').

philological_notes.note: Qere, 'and to him [we belong]'. The Ketiv is וְלֹא, 'and not'. The KJV translates the written text, 'and not we ourselves'. The meanings are almost opposite in force (a denial of self-creation versus a statement of ownership), but both are ancient, and the Masoretic tradition itself preserves both.

'The flock of his pasture': mar'it is the grazing place, and by extension the feeding that a shepherd gives. The royal shepherd image is common in Israel and the surrounding cultures; here it combines ownership and provision.
Plural in form, but with singular verbs and pronouns when it names YHWH; Metzudat David glosses 'God' as 'the one with all power' (baʿal hayekholet).

verses.translation_literal: Come [into] his gates with thanksgiving, [into] his courts with praise; give thanks to him, bless his name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Now come, through his gates with thanksgiving, into his courts with praise. Give thanks to him. Bless his name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm now becomes a procession. The crowd that was shouting in verse 1 has walked up to the Temple, and the verse moves them physically through two thresholds: first the gates (she'arim), then the courts (chatzerot), the open enclosures around the sanctuary where ordinary worshippers could stand. Stage it as a crowd passing through a narrow opening into a wide space. The Hebrew does not say 'enter into' twice, as the KJV does; there is only one verb, 'come', and the second noun simply follows it, which makes the movement run together.

Note the repeated word todah. It was the title in verse 1 and returns here as the entrance-gift, 'with thanksgiving', so the worshippers come bearing a thank-offering as well as words. Meiri reads it as thanksgiving for God's miracles. The final pair of verbs are not synonyms in the Hebrew: hodu is to confess or acknowledge what God has done, and barakhu is to bless, to speak good over his name. The KJV 'be thankful unto him' turns an action into a feeling; hodu is an act of speech. The BBE's 'doors' and 'house' soften the text, which has gates and courts, the public spaces of a sacred city.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yadah: to confess, acknowledge, give thanks aloud. It shares its root with todah, so verses 1 and 4 are tied by sound. 'Be thankful' (KJV) turns it into a mood.
'His courts': the open precincts of the sanctuary, where the people gathered. Ibn Ezra distributes the two terms: thanksgiving at the gates, praise in the courts.

verses.translation_literal: For good [is] YHWH; for ever [is] his covenant loyalty, and to generation and generation [is] his faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the LORD is good. His steadfast love has no end, and his faithfulness runs on from one generation to the next, and the next, and the next.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last verse supplies the 'for' (ki) that the whole psalm has been waiting for: why shout, why serve, why come? Because YHWH is good. Ibn Ezra says plainly that this is the thanksgiving itself, the very words the worshippers say. Let it come quietly after the noise of the opening, with the whole cast turned toward the same direction.

Two words carry the weight, and the KJV flattens both. Chesed is 'mercy' in the KJV, but it is covenant loyalty: the faithful commitment of a partner who is bound by an oath, and who does more than the minimum. Emunah is 'truth' in the KJV, but it means reliability, something that can be leaned on, from the root 'mn that gives us 'amen'. Rashi explains it as the faithfulness of one who makes a promise and keeps it; Radak as the promise made for the future. 'To generation and generation' is the Hebrew way of saying 'always' by repeating the unit, as we would say 'age after age'. Metzudat David adds the contrast that makes the verse land: the chesed of a human lasts only a while, but God's lasts to the end of all the generations.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, loyal love that goes beyond what is owed. 'Mercy' (KJV) names only one side of it. Metzudat David contrasts the lasting chesed of God with the chesed of a mortal.

Faithfulness, dependability, from the root of 'amen'. Rashi defines it as the promise that the one who promises believes and keeps; Radak as the promise of future good that remains valid through all the generations.
'Generation and generation': a repeated noun for the sense of 'all generations'.
